plot.label: Graphs of f(x) = log base 3 of x and g(x) = log base 3 of 9x; the graph of g lies 2 units above the graph of f

logarithmic-manipulation-s2.title: Values of $\ln x$

table.caption: Natural logarithms of 2, 3, 5 and 7, rounded to three decimal places

logarithmic-manipulation-s2.text: Use the table and the properties of logarithms, without a calculator.

why.correct: By the product property, $\log_3(9x) = \log_3 9 + \log_3 x = 2 + \log_3 x$. So $g(x) - f(x) = 2$, as the graph shows at $x = 1$, $3$ and $9$.
options: The factor $9$ inside the logarithm becomes $\log_3 9 = 2$ outside it.
Subtracting the inputs is not how the outputs compare; the gap is a constant.

items.q: Which transformation of the graph of $f$ gives the graph of $g$?
options: A vertical dilation by a factor of $9$

why.correct: $g(x) = 2 + f(x)$: every output of $f$ goes up by $2$.
options: A shift left would be $\log_3(x + 9)$; here $x$ is multiplied by $9$.
A vertical dilation multiplies outputs; $g(1) = 2$ while $9 f(1) = 0$.

items.q: The graph of $g$ can also be described as which transformation of the graph of $f$?
options: A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\frac{1}{9}$
A horizontal dilation by a factor of $9$
A vertical dilation by a factor of $2$

why.correct: $g(x) = f(9x)$: $g$ reaches each output of $f$ at an input $\frac{1}{9}$ as large, so the graph is squeezed toward the $y$-axis. For a logarithm, that horizontal dilation is the same as a vertical shift.
options: $f(9) = 2$ and $g(1) = 2$: each input is divided by $9$.
Multiplying the input by $9$ squeezes the graph; a factor of $9$ would stretch it.
A shift right would lower the graph; $g$ is above $f$.

mistakes.why: $9 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 3$ is the input of the logarithm; $\log_3 3 = 1$.

items.q: Let $k(x) = \log_3(x^2)$. Is $k(x) = 2f(x)$ for every $x$ in the domain of $k$?
options: Yes: the power property gives $\log_3(x^2) = 2\log_3 x$

why.correct: $k$ is defined for every $x \ne 0$, but $2f(x) = 2\log_3 x$ only for $x > 0$. They agree for $x > 0$; for $x < 0$, $k(x) = 2\log_3|x|$.
options: The power property needs $x > 0$; it does not hold at $x = -3$.
Sharing one point does not make two functions equal.
Product property: add the logarithms of the factors.
That multiplies $\ln 2$ by $\ln 3$; the logarithm of a product is a sum.
That is $(\ln 5)^2$; the power property gives $2\ln 5$, not a square.
That is $5\ln 5$; $25 = 5^2$, so the factor is $2$.
That is half of $\ln 5$, which would be $\ln \sqrt{5}$.
That is $\frac{\ln 5}{\ln 2}$; the logarithm of a quotient is a difference.
$\frac{\ln 7}{\ln 2}$, which lies between $2$ and $3$ as it should.

items.q: For $x > 0$, write $3\log_2 x - \log_2 5$ as a single logarithm.

mistakes.why: The $3$ is an exponent on $x$, not a factor: $3\log_2 x = \log_2 x^3$.
A difference of logarithms is the logarithm of a quotient, not of a difference.
Subtracting logarithms divides their inputs inside one logarithm; it does not divide two logarithms.

why.correct: Power property first: $3\log_2 x = \log_2 x^3$. Then the quotient property: $\log_2 x^3 - \log_2 5 = \log_2 \frac{x^3}{5}$.

items.q: Write $\ln(x^4) - \ln(x^2)$ as a single logarithm that is equal to it for every $x \ne 0$.

mistakes.why: $2\ln x$ equals $\ln(x^2)$ only for $x > 0$; at $x = -1$ it is undefined, while $\ln(x^2) = 0$.
A difference of logarithms is the logarithm of a quotient, not of a difference.
$\frac{x^4}{x^2} = x^2$, not $x$; and $\ln x$ is undefined for $x < 0$.

why.correct: Quotient property: $\ln(x^4) - \ln(x^2) = \ln \frac{x^4}{x^2} = \ln(x^2)$. Both sides are defined for every $x \ne 0$.

items.q: The function $f(x) = \log_4 x$ is a vertical dilation of $y = \log_2 x$. Write $f(x)$ as a constant times $\log_2 x$.

mistakes.why: Changing the base divides the whole logarithm by $\log_2 4$; it does not divide the input by $4$.

why.correct: Change of base: $\log_4 x = \frac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 4} = \frac{\log_2 x}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 x$. Check: $\log_4 16 = 2 = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 16$.

items.q: Which expression is equal to $\log_5(25x^3)$ for $x > 0$?

why.correct: Product property, then power property: $\log_5 25 + \log_5 x^3 = 2 + 3\log_5 x$.
options: The $2$ and the $3\log_5 x$ are added, not multiplied.
$25$ inside the logarithm becomes $\log_5 25 = 2$ outside it.
The exponent $3$ applies only to $x$, not to $25$.

mistakes.why: Adding logarithms multiplies their inputs: $4 \cdot 9 = 36$, not $4 + 9$.
That is the input $36$. The value is $\log_6 36 = 2$.

items.q: Use a calculator to find $\log_7 20$, correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is $\ln \frac{20}{7}$. Change of base divides the logarithms: $\frac{\ln 20}{\ln 7}$.

items.q: Which equation is true for every pair of positive numbers $x$ and $y$?

why.correct: The product property turns a product inside a logarithm into a sum outside it. There is no rule for a sum inside.
options: The quotient property gives $\log x - \log y$.
The power property is $\log(x^2) = 2\log x$; $(\log x)^2$ is a square of the logarithm.

items.q: Which expressions are equal to $3\ln 2$? Select every one that is.

options: $\ln 6 = \ln 2 + \ln 3$; the $3$ in $3\ln 2$ is an exponent, not a factor inside.

items.q: Consider $\log_b x$ for a base $b > 1$. Predict what happens to each quantity as the base $b$ increases.

variables.name: $\log_b 10$
variables.why: A larger base reaches $10$ with a smaller exponent: $\log_b 10 = \frac{\ln 10}{\ln b}$ and $\ln b$ grows.

variables.name: $\log_b \frac{1}{10}$
variables.why: $\log_b \frac{1}{10} = -\log_b 10$, which is negative and closer to $0$ as $b$ grows.

why.correct: By change of base, $\log_b x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$: every base gives a vertical dilation of $\ln x$, flatter for larger bases.

items.q: Put the steps for writing $2\log x + \log 3 - \log 5$ as a single logarithm in order.
options: State where it holds: $x > 0$, the domain of $\log x$

why.correct: Move coefficients into exponents first, then combine sums and differences; the result holds on the domain of the original.
